01Fault-finding

What it's doing, and why.

Most 12V problems on boats come back to a handful of causes. These are the ones we see most, and what is usually behind them.

What it's doingWhat's usually behind it

Sounder or GPS resets when the motor starts

UsuallyThe voltage dips while the starter is cranking. The cable feeding the electronics is too small, or they share the battery that starts the motor.

Battery flat after a week on the trailer

UsuallySomething is drawing power with everything switched off, or the battery is past it. A draw test shows which.

Lights flicker, or work when you wiggle a wire

UsuallyA corroded join or a poor earth, often inside a connector that looks fine from the outside.

A fuse that keeps blowing

UsuallyCable that has chafed through and is shorting, or a circuit being asked to carry more than it was built for.

Green crust on terminals and plugs

UsuallySalt and moisture in a joint that was never sealed. It travels up inside the cable, where you can't see it.

The radio is weak or noisy

UsuallyA poor power supply, a damaged aerial lead or a bad connection at the plug.

02What's covered

What we wire up.

New installs, upgrades and repairs on 12V systems. Everything is sized for the load, protected by its own fuse and labelled so it can be followed later.

  1. C01

    Dual-battery & lithium setups

    Start and house batteries kept separate, with charging matched to the battery type, so the motor always has enough to start.

  2. C02

    Switch panels & fuse blocks

    A proper panel with every circuit on its own fuse and a label you can read, in place of a row of mystery switches.

  3. C03

    Sounders, GPS & chartplotters

    Units mounted where you can see them, transducers set up to read cleanly, and power fed from a fused supply.

  4. C04

    VHF radios & aerials

    Radio, aerial and coax fitted and routed properly, so the set gets full power and a clear signal when it matters.

  5. C05

    Bow-mount electric motors

    Heavy cable sized for the length of the run, a breaker at the battery and a plug at the bow that stays dry.

  6. C06

    LED, nav & deck lighting

    Navigation lights you can rely on, plus deck, cabin and underwater lighting on their own switched circuits.

  7. C07

    Bilge pumps & float switches

    Pumps wired with an automatic float switch and a manual override, on a circuit that stays live when everything else is off.

  8. C08

    Rewires & fault-finding

    Dropouts, flat batteries and corroded joins traced back to the cause, or stripped out and started again when that is the better fix.

03Try it yourself

Will it get full voltage?

Thin cable over a long run loses voltage before it reaches the gear. That is why a sounder resets or a pump runs slow. Put in your own numbers and see how much is lost.

5 A

How much current the gear draws. A sounder is 1 to 3 A, a bilge pump about 5 A, a bow-mount electric 40 A or more.

4 m

One way, from the battery to the gear, following the route the cable takes.

mm²

The copper cross-section, not the outside width of the insulation.

Voltage lost on the way

2.4%

03%10%

0.29 V lost, so a 12.6 V battery delivers 12.3 V at the gear.

Good for electronics and nav lights

This cable is big enough for this load over this run.

A guide only. It assumes copper cable on a 12V system and counts the run out and back. Common marine practice is to keep the loss to 3% or less for electronics and navigation lights, and 10% or less for everything else. Cable also has to be rated for the current, and the fuse sized to protect the cable.

04The standard

Behind the dash, before and after.

What we find

  • Untinned cable that has gone black inside the insulation
  • Twisted joins wrapped in tape
  • One fuse feeding everything, or no fuse at all
  • Connectors sitting down in the bilge
  • Nothing labelled, and no way to trace it

What we leave

  • Tinned marine cable, sized for the load and the run
  • Crimped, heat-shrunk and sealed joins
  • Every circuit on its own fuse
  • Connections kept up high and dry
  • Labels at the panel and at the gear

05Good to know

Electrical questions.

Can't see yours here? Ask it in the booking form or give us a call.

Can you install electronics I have already bought?

Usually, yes. Tell us the make and model when you book so we can check it suits the boat and turn up with the right cable, fuses and fittings.

Do I need a second battery?

It depends on what you run. A sounder and a few lights are fine on one battery. Add a fridge, bigger screens or long days at anchor and a separate house battery stops the electronics from flattening the one that starts the motor. Tell us what you run and we will tell you straight.

Should the old wiring be repaired or replaced?

If the cable is sound and the problem is a few bad joins, a repair is fine. If the cable has gone black inside the insulation, or years of add-ons have no fusing, a rewire usually costs less than chasing faults one at a time. We will tell you which way we would go, and why, before any work starts.

How long does an install take?

A single sounder or a set of lights is a short job. A dual-battery system or a full rewire takes longer. You will get a realistic timeframe with your quote.
